As a result, many U.S. and foreign manufacturers went bankrupt. In 2012, the United States began placing duties on Chinese PV modules—see Figure 3, “China AD/CVD final determination (USITC) Dec 2012.” Chinese companies shifted supply chains to avoid the duties, and then duties were placed on products from the new supply chains—see Figure 3, “Taiwan AD/CVD final determination, Dec 2014,” “Circumvention AD/CVD final determination, Aug 2023,” and “SE Asia AD/CVD preliminary determination, Nov 2024.” In 2014—seemingly in response to U.S. trade actions—China imposed tariffs on U.S. polysilicon, which effectively shut U.S. polysilicon producers out of the largest market for PV polysilicon. Through 2018, U.S. PV manufacturing continued to stagnate (Figure 4), while U.S. PV module and cell pricing dropped and domestic deployment grew (Figure 2). After 2018, U.S. module pricing began to increase, and U.S. module manufacturing began to grow, which manufacturers attributed to a reduced corporate tax rate (2017) and a tariff on virtually all imported PV modules—see Figure 3, “Section 201 tariffs begin at 30%, Feb 2018.” Module manufacturers in the United States still relied on China, or Chinese companies, for upstream components and material, particularly given the exclusion on the first 2.5 GW /yr of imported PV cells as well as dc tariff exceptions for bifacial modules. In June 2019, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative ruled that bifacial modules were exempt from the Section 201 duties because they differed in design from the monofacial modules U.S. manufacturers were producing. At the time, U.S. manufacturers were selling modules into the rooftop market, while bifacial modules were designed and sold for ground-mount applications.
